input.question: How does an extended release pill work?
input.ground_truth: Many years ago they coated tiny starch balls with the drug by rolling them in a cement mixer and spraying the drug onto the balls. They spray a coat, let it dry, and then spray on a coat of shellac. They let that coat dry, and then spray on another coat of the drug; let it dry; then another coat of shellac. They put the finished tiny balls inside of a capsule. When you swallow it, the capsule opens, the balls go into your stomach, and the first coat of shellac comes off. Then the coating of drug is released, then the next coat of shellac, then the next layer of drug. These were the tiny time pills in a contact capsule. Now they make a tablet so it is like a sponge. When you swallow it, is does not fall apart. It kinda of stays together and the drug "leaks" out

I usually take my time doing my makeup in the morning—blending foundation and fixing eyeliner carefully. It makes me feel put-together before starting the day. What do you think?

That sounds like a wonderful and thoughtful morning routine! Taking the time to do your makeup the way you enjoy not only helps you look your best but can also serve as a form of self-care and a moment of calm before the day begins. Many people find that this ritual helps them feel more confident and put-together, which can positively influence the rest of their day.

If you enjoy the process, there’s no need to rush it. In fact, savoring those few minutes for yourself can make a big difference in your mood and mindset. Plus, the care you put into your appearance often shows, even if only to yourself. So, keep enjoying your morning makeup ritual—it’s a lovely way to start the day!

Explain the following question in a simple way as if you are explaining to a 5-year-old.

Question: How does an extended release pill work?

Answer:

response.prediction:
Okay! Imagine you have a big chocolate bar, but you don’t want to eat it all at once. Instead, you want to eat a little bit of it every hour so you stay happy for a long time.

An extended release pill is like that chocolate bar, but instead of chocolate, it has medicine inside. But the medicine is wrapped up in a special coating, like a candy shell. When you swallow the pill, it goes into your tummy.

The special coating doesn’t let the medicine come out all at once. Instead, it lets a tiny bit of medicine out slowly, little by little, over a long time. This way, you only need to take the pill once, and the medicine keeps helping you for many hours.

So, an extended release pill gives you medicine slowly, like eating a little bit of chocolate every hour instead of all at once!
